svg.text: The Deck Log and Written Reports

g.text: Why the wording matters
The log is evidence. After a casualty it is read years later by people who were not there —
investigators, surveyors, lawyers and the court. Write it so it still makes sense to them.
Do
Record facts, times and observations.
Use UTC or state the time zone used.
Write in ink, at the time, in sequence.
Name who did what, and who was told.
Correct an error with a single line through
it, the correction beside it, and initials.
Do not
Do not record opinion, blame or a cause.
Do not leave gaps or blank lines.
Do not erase, overwrite or use correction
fluid — an altered log destroys its value.
Do not write it up later from memory.
Do not use vague words like "some" or "soon".
Structure of a statement or incident report
1 · What the ship was doing before it happened 2 · What happened, in time order, with positions
3 · What was done in response, and by whom 4 · Who was informed, and when 5 · Attachments and log extracts
